implementation_notes: Spring Security is the dominant Java realization: an AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext> is the Policy and the AuthorizationFilter (HTTP) or the method-security interceptor behind @PreAuthorize/@PostAuthorize is the Guard; rules are declared per request matcher and the last matching rule decides, with anyRequest().denyAll() making the default explicit. The manager receives a Supplier<Authentication> plus the request object - exactly the (subject, action, resource) triple - and a custom manager is attached with access(...); it may publish an AuthorizationDeniedEvent and the ExceptionTranslationFilter turns the thrown AccessDeniedException into 403. What replaces the classic structure: the servlet filter chain and method interceptors replace hand-written guard wrappers, so only managers, matchers and rules are written. Hand-roll a policy object only when no framework interceptor can reach the resource (batch jobs, non-Servlet contexts).
pitfalls: The AuthorizationFilter runs last in the security filter chain: filters registered before it execute unguarded, and all dispatches (FORWARD, ERROR) are authorized again - permit them deliberately or requests fail twice.
@PreAuthorize is not invoked for internal self-invocation of a method inside the same bean; do not rely on method security for intra-bean calls.
The authorization context is fetched lazily from the SecurityContextHolder; storing an Authentication in a long-lived manager and reusing it after logout keeps granting rights (TOCTOU).

variants.name: java.security.Policy + AccessController (legacy Security Manager)
variants.implementation_notes: The JDK itself once implemented this pattern: java.security.Policy was the Policy component - its implies method answers whether a ProtectionDomain gets a Permission - and AccessController was the Guard that checked the installed policy before a security-sensitive operation, with policy files assigning permissions to code sources. The Security Manager and this class are deprecated for removal since Java 17 and have no replacement, so this realization is for understanding or maintaining legacy systems only; new code should use the Spring Security variant or an external policy decision point. What replaces the classic structure: the installed Policy singleton plus a check call at every protected operation replaced explicit guard objects - exactly the pattern's shape, which is why it is documented as the JVM's built-in instance of it.
pitfalls: SecurityManager and Policy are deprecated for removal and may behave differently or disappear across JDK releases; do not start new work on them.
Removing a checkPermission call leaves the operation unguarded rather than failing closed, and the default policy grants almost nothing - coverage must be reviewed like any hand-written guard.
